title: Worker exposure: Technical susceptibility differs from displacement
desc: Combines historical adjustment and recent AI-exposure estimates while emphasizing age effects, mobility and sensitivity to controls.

kps.k: The cluster distinguishes technological exposure from realised displacement and uneven labour-market adjustment.
kps.d: Its substantive contribution is empirical rather than predictive: historical automation can reduce occupational persistence while workers adjust through other jobs or migration, whereas contemporary LLM-exposure measures do not themselves establish job losses. In GPTs are GPTs, salary coefficients in exposure regressions are positive, but only two of three carry significance markers; the wage data come from May 2021. These associations identify characteristics of exposed occupations, not observed displacement, productivity gains or causal AI effects.

qs.q: We also include annualized wages from the BLS-OES survey in May 2021.
qs.a: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Telephone automation illustrates persistent, age-specific costs rather than frictionless movement into equivalent work.
kps.d: Answering the Call of Automation compares incumbent female operators’ decade-later outcomes with matched controls around cities’ first telephone cutovers. One table estimates an 8.1–8.7-percentage-point decline in remaining a telephone-industry operator. A separate sample estimates a 2.9–3.6-point decline in employment overall, rising to 7.5–8.7 points among operators aged 26 or older. Across displayed tables, the probability of declining in occupation-score decile rises by about 7.9–10.5 points. The samples and outcomes differ, occupation scores are not individual wages, and these historical estimates do not directly forecast AI’s effects.

kps.k: Adjustment through mobility and occupational substitution can coexist with employment losses.
kps.d: The telephone-automation study estimates a 3.0–3.7-percentage-point increase in moves exceeding 25 miles, while adjacent telephone-industry jobs provide only limited offsets. Separate population tables show employed white, American-born women aged 16–20 moving away from operator work and toward waitress work, alongside lower occupation scores. Those conditional occupational shares neither measure overall employment nor track only displaced operators. For workforce analysis, the practical implication is to examine destination jobs and geographic moves alongside headcounts; the excerpts do not evaluate a particular transition policy.

kps.k: Recent AI-exposure estimates suggest younger-worker vulnerability, but joint controls substantially qualify that pattern.
kps.d: In the supplied August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine?, the no-controls panel reports quintile-4 coefficients of −0.145 for ages 22–25 and −0.064 for ages 26–30, both statistically significant. Neither supplied panel jointly controlling for interest-rate exposure, college share and work from home marks any exposure coefficient as significant. This specification sensitivity does not establish either a robust causal displacement effect or the absence of an effect. The study balances firms observed since January 2018, but the fragments do not identify the precise estimation period or outcome units, so the coefficients cannot safely become percentage job-loss claims. Its younger-worker pattern and the telephone study’s older-incumbent losses concern different technologies, populations and outcomes, not a direct contradiction.

qs.q: The panels differ only in the occupational controls included: none (A); interest rate exposure (Zens et al., 2020) (B); college share from the 2017 ACS (C); the work-from-home measure of Lambert and Schindler (2026) (D); teleworkability (Dingel and Neiman, 2020) (E); and interest rate, college share, and work from home jointly (F).
qs.a: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (August 2026 revision) · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Incomplete excerpts prevent broader conclusions about productivity, legal staffing or licensing—and do not establish a source-level disagreement.
kps.d: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects supplies no reliably interpretable substantive result here; its title cannot establish small effects. The education-productivity experiment supplies participant characteristics, not productivity outcomes. Missing outcome labels likewise prevent conclusions about hierarchy or knowledge utilisation from the legal-services study, or wage effects from most licensing coefficients. The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market supplies 1980–2010 wage-growth associations, not direct evidence of generative AI’s effects. These limits leave the cluster focused on heterogeneous adjustment and evidentiary distinctions, without supporting a quantified legal-employment forecast or a policy prescription.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition’s core distinction between technical exposure and realised displacement, and materially develop it with evidence on heterogeneous labour-market adjustment. Contemporary LLM-exposure research measures occupational susceptibility or associations rather than observed job loss, while the supplied recent-employment study shows that apparent younger-worker effects are sensitive to occupational controls. Historical telephone automation adds a concrete extension: displacement can reduce occupational persistence and overall employment unevenly—especially for older incumbents—while also prompting migration and occupational substitution rather than frictionless movement into equivalent work. Material internal variation is mainly evidentiary, not oppositional: some sources directly support the distinction; the telephone study builds on it through historical adjustment evidence; and several truncated tables remain unclear because missing outcomes or narrative prevent any substantive position. These records are a curated selection and do not establish how prevalent these views are across academia or research generally.

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources cannot be positioned substantively relative to the proposition that technical susceptibility differs from realised displacement. Both provide incomplete regression-table material without enough surrounding argument or outcome information to determine whether they distinguish exposure, displacement and adjustment. Their shared relevance is methodological: they reinforce the synthesis’s caution against drawing labour-market conclusions from coefficients whose dependent variables, headings or key estimates are missing. There is limited internal variation in why interpretation fails. The legal-services source provides sample and inference details but lacks the outcome labels needed to interpret employment-related coefficients; the occupational-licensing source identifies a log-wage outcome in one table, but the central licensing estimate is truncated and the material does not address technology or displacement. Thus, neither source supports nor contradicts the proposition on the supplied evidence. Because these are curated sources, this assessment does not imply a general pre-2015 consensus or lack of one.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source supports the proposition’s core distinction between technical susceptibility and realised displacement, but only indirectly. It reports historical wage-growth regressions across occupation-industry cells for 1980–2010, with controls and methodological qualifications, rather than observing AI-driven job loss or forecasting generative AI’s labour-market effects. This makes it consistent with the cluster’s caution that occupational characteristics and historical associations should not be converted into causal displacement claims. Materially, however, the excerpt does not address several other parts of the proposition—such as age-specific effects, geographic mobility, occupational substitution or contemporary LLM exposure—so its support is narrow and evidentiary rather than a full confirmation of the cluster’s account. Because this time-period facet contains only one curated source, no broader position or prevalence within the period can be inferred.

elens.an: The selected sources from this period collectively accept the proposition that technical exposure must not be equated with realised displacement, while materially developing its account of uneven adjustment. The LLM-exposure study supports the evidentiary boundary directly: its regressions associate occupational exposure scores with earlier automation measures and May 2021 wages, but do not estimate causal job losses. The telephone-automation study adds historical evidence about what realised displacement can look like, including reduced occupational persistence, employment losses concentrated among older incumbents, downward occupational movement and increased migration. The principal internal variation is therefore in evidentiary role rather than direction: one source measures contemporary susceptibility without observed displacement, whereas the other documents historical displacement and adjustment but cannot by itself forecast generative AI’s effects. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all research published in 2023–2024.

The sole supplied source record for this curated 2025 facet contains only truncated statistical tables without usable headings, explanatory notes or substantive narrative. It therefore cannot be determined whether the source accepts or disputes the proposition that technical susceptibility must be distinguished from realised displacement and uneven labour-market adjustment. Nor can the source reliably support claims about age effects, mobility, occupational substitution or sensitivity to controls. This is an evidentiary limitation rather than source-level disagreement with the proposition.

The usable 2026 evidence supports the proposition that technical exposure should not be equated with realised displacement and that apparent labour-market effects vary by age and specification. The August 2026 revision of “Canaries in the Coal Mine?” reports comparatively negative high-exposure coefficients for younger workers in specifications without occupational controls, but those estimates become smaller and statistically insignificant when interest-rate exposure, college share and working from home are jointly controlled. This supports an age-specific vulnerability signal while cautioning against interpreting it as a robust causal job-loss estimate. Internal variation arises from evidentiary completeness rather than substantive disagreement: the randomized education-productivity excerpt contains participant characteristics but no productivity or employment outcomes, so its position is indeterminate and it cannot test the proposition. Given that these are curated sources, this assessment characterizes only the supplied evidence and does not indicate how prevalent either view is among 2026 researchers.
